questions.question: A boy rubs a rubber balloon briskly on his dry hair. Afterward the balloon and his hair pull toward each other, for one of them now carries a negative charge and the other a positive one. What has the rubbing done?
questions.answer: Moved electrons from his hair onto the balloon
choices: Moved electrons from his hair onto the balloon
Moved electrons from the balloon onto his hair
Moved protons from the balloon onto his hair
Moved protons from his hair onto the balloon
questions.context: Hair gives up electrons more easily than rubber, so the rubbing carries electrons from the hair onto the balloon: the balloon ends up with extra electrons and a negative charge, and the hair, short of electrons, is left positive. Protons stay fast in the nucleus of every atom. Rubbing makes no new charge; it only moves electrons from one thing to another.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons on electric forces (curriculum line G8.P9, NGSS MS-PS2-3) teach charging by rubbing as electrons moving from one object to the other, with the balloon and hair as the classic case.

questions.question: A girl rubs two balloons on her hair, one after the other, and hangs them from the same hook on long threads. Instead of hanging straight down side by side, the two balloons swing apart and stay apart. What pushes them apart?
questions.answer: Like charges, which push each other away
choices: Like charges, which push each other away
Unlike charges, which push each other away
Like magnetic poles, which push each other away
Unlike magnetic poles, which push each other away
questions.context: Rubbing on the same hair gives both balloons the same kind of electric charge, and like charges repel, across the gap with nothing touching. The more charge each balloon carries, the harder the push, and it weakens as they swing apart. A rubbed balloon is no magnet, and unlike charges attract, just as unlike magnetic poles do.
questions.grade_note: NGSS MS-PS2-5 asks 8th graders for evidence that charged objects push on each other without touching, and like charges repel is the rule they learn (curriculum line G8.P9).

questions.question: A boy rubs a balloon on his hair and holds it against a painted wall. When he lets go, the balloon stays there, though the wall itself carries no charge. What holds the balloon to the wall?
questions.answer: Its charge draws the wall's opposite charges nearer
choices: Its charge draws the wall's opposite charges nearer
Its charge flows into the wall and holds it there
Air pressure pins it flat against the wall
The rubbing has turned it into a weak magnet
questions.context: The balloon's charge pushes the like charges in the wall's atoms a little way back and draws the opposite ones a little nearer, so the surface just under the balloon carries a slight opposite charge, and unlike charges attract. The nearer opposite charge pulls harder than the farther like charge pushes, because electric forces weaken with distance. Pressed to a metal door, the balloon soon loses its charge into the metal and falls.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons on electric forces use the balloon stuck to a wall to show that a charged object attracts a neutral one by shifting its charges (curriculum line G8.P9, NGSS MS-PS2-5).

questions.question: A compass on a desk points north, lined up with Earth's magnetism. A girl slides a small bar magnet to within a few centimetres of it, and the needle swings round to point at the magnet instead. Why does so small a magnet win out over Earth here?
questions.answer: It is close, and magnetism fades with distance
choices: It is close, and magnetism fades with distance
It is a stronger magnet than the whole of Earth
Its magnetism is a different kind from Earth's
It shields the needle from Earth's magnetism
questions.context: Earth as a whole is a vastly stronger magnet, but its field at the surface is weak, and a magnet's field grows weaker very fast with distance. A few centimetres from the small magnet its field is many times Earth's, so the needle follows it; carried across the room, its field falls far below Earth's, and the needle swings back to north. The small magnet blocks nothing: its field and Earth's simply add, and the needle lines up with the sum.
questions.grade_note: NGSS PS2.B (MS-PS2-3) teaches 8th graders that the size of a magnetic force depends on the magnets' strength and on the distance between the objects.

questions.question: William Gilbert, an English physician, shaped a lodestone into a ball he called a terrella, a little Earth. Over it he held a small magnetised needle, free to turn. The needle lined up with the ball's poles and tipped down toward its surface, more steeply nearer the poles, just as a needle free to tilt does on Earth. What did Gilbert conclude in De Magnete, in 1600?
questions.answer: Earth itself is a giant magnet
choices: Earth itself is a giant magnet
The Pole Star draws every needle north
A magnetic island lies at the North Pole
A needle seeks the north by its own nature
questions.context: A needle on the terrella pointed to the ball's own poles and dipped the way compass needles had been found to dip on Earth, so Gilbert reasoned that Earth works the same way: it is itself a great magnet, and its magnetism lines up every compass. The pull of the Pole Star and a magnetic island at the pole were older explanations that he set aside, and his needle followed whatever magnet it was near, not the north.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons on magnetism teach that Earth is a giant magnet that turns a compass, and Gilbert's De Magnete (1600) is where the idea was first argued from experiment.

questions.question: A compass needle is a small magnet, and the end marked N swings round toward the far north. It points toward the North Magnetic Pole, a spot in the Arctic where Earth's magnetism points straight down into the ground. Judged by how magnets push and pull, what kind of magnetic pole is that spot?
questions.answer: A south pole, since unlike poles attract
choices: A south pole, since unlike poles attract
A north pole, since like poles attract
A north pole, since it lies in the far north
Neither, since plain iron draws either end
questions.context: The N end of a compass is its north-seeking pole, and unlike poles attract, so the magnetic pole that draws it in the Arctic must be a south pole. It is called the North Magnetic Pole for where it lies, not for its kind. Plain iron would draw either end of the needle, yet the needle's S end always turns away to the south.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches like and unlike poles and Earth as a magnet; the south magnetic pole in the far north is the classic case that puts the two together.

questions.question: Hans Christian Oersted held a wire just above a compass needle during a lecture at the University of Copenhagen in April 1820. When he joined the wire to a battery and current flowed, the needle swung away from north. What did the needle show?
questions.answer: The current in the wire made a magnetic field
choices: The current in the wire made a magnetic field
The needle's own field made a current in the wire
The battery's metal plates were magnets themselves
Some current leaked from the wire into the needle
questions.context: The current itself made a magnetic field around the wire, and that field turned the needle. With the circuit broken the needle settled back, though the battery's copper and zinc plates, which are not magnetic, stayed where they were; and the needle sat under glass, out of reach of any current. It was the first proof that electricity and magnetism are linked, and later tests that year showed the field runs in circles around the wire.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons on electromagnetism open with Oersted's needle of 1820, the first evidence that an electric current makes a magnetic field (curriculum line G8.P9).

questions.question: A student winds a long insulated wire 20 times around an iron nail, leaving the rest of the wire loose, and joins its ends to a battery. The nail lifts six paper clips. She then makes one change at a time, to see which lets the nail lift more. Which change will do it?
questions.answer: Winding more of the loose wire around the nail
choices: Winding more of the loose wire around the nail
Turning the battery round to reverse the current
Swapping the iron nail for a copper nail
Pulling the nail out, leaving the coil alone
questions.context: An electromagnet grows stronger with more turns of wire and with more current, so winding the loose wire onto the nail, with the same wire and the same current, lets it lift more. Turning the battery round only swaps the magnet's north and south ends. The iron core is what makes a coil strong, up to thousands of times stronger than the coil alone, while copper is not magnetic and adds nothing; Joseph Henry wound silk-covered wire in layer on layer for just this reason.
questions.grade_note: NGSS MS-PS2-3 names this very test for 8th graders: the effect of the number of turns of wire on the strength of an electromagnet.

questions.question: An electromagnetic lock holds a shop's back door shut. A coil in the door frame grips a steel plate on the door with a pull of about 1,200 pounds, and the lock has no moving parts. What happens to that grip if the building's power fails?
questions.answer: It vanishes at once, so the door comes free
choices: It vanishes at once, so the door comes free
It holds on, so the door stays locked
It fades slowly, so the door comes free in hours
It turns to a push, so the door is flung open
questions.context: The coil is a magnet only while current flows through it, so the moment the power stops, its grip is gone and the door opens with a push. That makes the lock fail-safe: in a fire alarm or a power cut, nobody is trapped inside. A scrapyard crane drops its load of steel the same way, when the current to its electromagnet is switched off.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches that an electromagnet works only while current flows, which is what makes it useful in locks, cranes and switches (curriculum line G8.P9).
